title: India–China: Economy and Multilateral Rivalry

cards.b:
India and China are neighbours, Asia's two largest populations and two of its biggest economies. Their trade is large. Their strategic trust is small. That gap is the heart of this lesson.

Exam questions ask three things: (1) why India depends on Chinese goods even while distrusting China; (2) how the two compete in the neighbourhood, the Indian Ocean and global institutions; and (3) where they cooperate, as in BRICS, SCO and climate talks.

Keep one idea in mind: China treats India as a regional rival that should stay inside South Asia. India wants to be treated as a great power in its own right.

In FY2024-25 bilateral trade was about $128 billion. India's deficit with China crossed $99 billion, its largest with any country (figures as of 2025).

China is the key supplier of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), mobile phone parts, solar cells, lithium-ion batteries, tunnel-boring machines and, importantly, rare earth magnets. When China curbed rare earth magnet exports in April 2025, Indian car and electronics makers were hit within weeks. Some licences were later granted to Indian firms.

The lesson Indian planners took: dependence on one supplier is a strategic weakness. The answer is PLI schemes, the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) and supply-chain partnerships with Japan, Australia and the US.

• April 2020, Press Note 3: investment from land-border countries needs government approval. It was aimed at stopping opportunistic Chinese takeovers during Covid.
  • App bans from June 2020 (TikTok, WeChat and over 300 others eventually) under Section 69A of the IT Act.
  • RCEP exit (November 2019): India walked out partly over fear of Chinese goods swamping its market.
  • Belt and Road: India is the main large state that refuses to join, saying the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) passes through Indian territory in PoK.

As of 2026 the guardrails are being loosened, selectively. The Cabinet approved changes to Press Note 3 on 10 March 2026. Since 1 May 2026, investors from land-border countries can hold up to 10% non-controlling stakes through the automatic route, and some manufacturing sectors get faster approvals. Early approvals were small: about 29 projects worth ₹4,900 crore by August 2026.

Analysts call it selective de-risking, not decoupling.

The 'string of pearls' idea (from a 2004 US study) describes Chinese-linked ports ringing the Indian Ocean. China says they are commercial. India sees possible military use. China's base at Djibouti opened in 2017.

India answers with its own offers: Neighbourhood First (2014), the SAGAR doctrine (2015) which became MAHASAGAR (2025), lines of credit, the Colombo Security Conclave, and port projects at Chabahar and Sittwe.

Smaller states play both sides. They take Chinese money and Indian security and trade, and they bargain with each.

cards.h: Belt and Road versus India's offers
cards.b:
China launched the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in 2013. India boycotted the Belt and Road Forums of 2017 and 2019.

India's answers are mostly connectivity with partners: the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) with Russia and Iran, the Chabahar port in Iran, the Kaladan project in Myanmar, the India–Middle East–Europe Corridor (IMEC) announced at the G20 in 2023, and the Asia-Africa Growth Corridor with Japan.

India says its model is demand-driven and respects sovereignty. Critics note that India's own projects are slower, and several (Chabahar, IMEC, Kaladan) have faced delays from war, sanctions and instability.

cards.h: BRICS, SCO and AIIB: cooperate and compete
cards.b:
Both sit in BRICS (2009), SCO (India joined 2017) and the AIIB (2016, where China is the largest shareholder and India second). Both are in the New Development Bank.

  • BRICS: China wants it as an anti-West bloc and pushes expansion. India supports expansion in a measured way and has said it does not want de-dollarisation. India chaired BRICS in 2026 and the New Delhi summit (12–13 September) adopted a consensus declaration.
  • SCO: India refused to sign the 2018 Qingdao text over BRI. At Tianjin in 2025 the declaration condemned the Pahalgam attack. The 2026 summit was in Bishkek (31 August–1 September).
  • Climate and trade: both back developing-country positions, though India differs from China on loss of its own coal and manufacturing space.

cards.h: Blocking India at the top table
cards.b:
• NSG: China led opposition to India's membership in 2016, insisting on non-NPT criteria applying equally to Pakistan.
  • UN 1267 sanctions: China placed 'technical holds' on listing Masood Azhar until 2019, when he was finally listed.
  • UNSC reform: China backs Africa and Latin America more than a permanent seat for India, and does not endorse India's claim.
  • Standards and values: China pushes its own tech standards, a rival 'Global Development Initiative' and a Global Security Initiative. India offers DPI (UPI, Aadhaar-style models) and the Voice of the Global South summits.

Both claim to speak for the Global South. This competition is about leadership, not just trade.

Hedgers say India should deepen trade with China to grow, while arming and partnering to deter. Hawks say any dependence is a lever China will use, so India should restrict Chinese capital and tech, as in the app bans.

A third view, from Shyam Saran (How China Sees India and the World, 2022), is that India must understand China's own strategic culture and negotiate from strength, not reaction.

Structural point: India's manufacturing push (PLI, electronics assembly) still needs Chinese parts. India's electronics exports have grown, yet they rely on Chinese components and sometimes Chinese technicians. Reported 2025 curbs on specialty fertilisers and tunnel-boring machines, along with the rare earth curbs, showed how supply can be used as pressure.

Where India has gained leverage: it is among the world's top five economies by 2025–26 estimates, a favoured 'China plus one' site (Apple supply chains moved strongly to India in 2024–25), and an FTA partner of the UK, EFTA and the EU (concluded January 2026).

Where it is exposed: a deficit near $100 billion, tech and critical-mineral dependence, and a smaller defence-industrial base.

Recent steps: loosening Press Note 3 within limits; resuming direct flights and border trade; Modi–Xi meeting at Tianjin; and tariff pressure from the US pushing both Delhi and Beijing to stabilise. A reported China complaint at the WTO against India's EV and battery subsidies in 2025 shows that disputes continue.

For the exam, cite one metric (the deficit), one rule (Press Note 3), one forum (BRICS or SCO) and one 2026 change.

"India-China relations are marked by trade growth and strategic rivalry. Discuss." (typical)
"What are the implications of China's Belt and Road Initiative for India?" (typical)
"Compare India and China's roles in BRICS and SCO." (typical)

Structure: (1) trade numbers and dependence; (2) Indian guardrails and their recent easing; (3) BRI, CPEC and the neighbourhood contest; (4) multilateral cooperation and rivalry (BRICS, SCO, AIIB, NSG, 1267); (5) assessment: managed rivalry; (6) way forward: diversify, build capacity, keep dialogue.

A short table, cooperation versus competition, scores well.

quiz.q: India's trade deficit with China in FY2024-25 was roughly:
quiz.w: The deficit was about $99 billion, India's largest with any country.

quiz.q: Press Note 3 (April 2020) required government approval for FDI from:
o: Countries sharing a land border with India
quiz.w: It covers all land-border countries, in practice mainly China.

quiz.q: India withdrew from RCEP negotiations in:
quiz.w: India decided not to join at Bangkok in November 2019.

quiz.q: India's stated objection to the Belt and Road Initiative centres on:
o: CPEC passing through Indian territory in PoK
quiz.w: CPEC runs through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, which India claims.

quiz.q: The term 'string of pearls' refers to:
o: Chinese-linked ports ringing the Indian Ocean
quiz.w: It describes Chinese port interests and possible military access around the Indian Ocean.

quiz.q: India's MAHASAGAR vision, announced in 2025, builds on which earlier doctrine?
quiz.w: SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region) was announced in 2015.

quiz.q: In which year did China place technical holds on listing Masood Azhar at UN 1267, until he was finally listed?
quiz.w: He was listed in May 2019 after repeated holds.

quiz.q: India joined the SCO as a full member in:
quiz.w: India and Pakistan were admitted at Astana in June 2017.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'How China Sees India and the World' (2022)?
What did the Cabinet's 2026 change to Press Note 3 mainly allow?
o: Land-border investors up to 10% non-controlling stakes via the automatic route
A ban on all Chinese firms
quiz.w: It allows limited, non-controlling investor stakes automatically, with faster approvals in some manufacturing sectors.
